title: A Peach Basket in a Gym
bigQuestion: How did one cold room in Springfield, Massachusetts, give the world a new sport?

story.title: The Room Under the Running Track
story.kicker: A teacher in a snowy town needs an indoor game that will not break the windows.
paragraphs: It is December 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts. Snow covers the fields outside the YMCA Training School. Inside, a young teacher named James Naismith stands in a small gym. A running track circles the room above him, like a balcony.

His class of young men is restless. They have done gymnastics exercises all fall. Now they want a real game. Football is too rough for a hard wooden floor. A hard-thrown ball could crack the tall windows.
His boss, Luther Gulick, has asked him to make up a new indoor game. Naismith thinks about games he played as a boy in Canada. He decides the goal should sit high, above the players' heads.

He asks a building worker for two boxes. The worker comes back with two old peach baskets. Naismith nails one to the balcony rail at each end of the gym. The rail is ten feet above the floor. A new game is about to begin.
story.think: Why do you think the size and shape of that small winter gym mattered so much to the new game?

lessons.title: Stone Rings in Old Mexico
lessons.mainIdea: Long before basketball, people in Mexico and Central America played a ball game on stone courts, but it is a separate story.
reading: People in Mexico and Central America played a *ballgame* more than 3,000 years ago. Archaeologists found one of the oldest known courts at Paso de la Amada, in Chiapas, Mexico. It dates to about 1650 BCE.

The players used a heavy ball made of *rubber*. Rubber starts as a milky liquid inside certain tropical trees. Later courts had stone rings set high on the side walls. The Great Ball Court at Chichen Itza, in Mexico, is the largest one known.

A high ring sounds a little like a basketball hoop. But historians have found no link between the two. James Naismith did not copy the old game. The two ideas grew far apart, in different times and places.

words.d: an old game of Mexico and Central America, played with a rubber ball on a stone court
a bouncy material made from the sap of certain trees
a scientist who learns about the past by digging up old places and objects

lessons.title: The YMCA Builds Gyms
lessons.mainIdea: The YMCA began in London in 1844 and built gyms in American cities to train the body, mind and spirit.
reading: The *YMCA* stands for the Young Men's Christian Association. George Williams started it in London, England, in 1844. It was a place for young workers who had moved to the city.
The first YMCA in the United States opened in Boston in 1851. Over time, many YMCAs added a *gymnasium*, or gym. Leaders wanted young men to grow strong in body as well as in mind and faith.

The YMCA used a triangle as a sign. Its three sides stood for spirit, mind and body. Luther Gulick helped make that sign well known. The training school in Springfield even called its newspaper The Triangle.

words.d: the Young Men's Christian Association, started in London in 1844
a large indoor room for exercise and games; gym for short

lessons.title: A Winter Problem
lessons.mainIdea: In the fall of 1891, Luther Gulick asked James Naismith to invent an indoor game for a restless winter class.
reading: In 1891 the school in Springfield was called the International YMCA Training School. Today it is Springfield College. It trained men to lead YMCA programs. *Luther Gulick* ran its physical education classes.

New England winters are long and cold. Football and baseball moved off the frozen fields. Indoors, students did marching and gymnastics exercises. One class of older students found these exercises dull and grew restless.
Gulick handed that class to James Naismith. He asked Naismith to create a new game that could be played indoors. It had to fit a small gym. It had to be safe on a hard floor and near glass windows.

words.d: the leader of physical education at the YMCA Training School who asked Naismith for a new game
school lessons about exercise, health and games

lessons.title: A Teacher from Canada
lessons.mainIdea: James Naismith was born in Ontario, Canada, in 1861 and came to Springfield in 1890.
reading: James Naismith was born in 1861 near Almonte, a town in Ontario, Canada. Both of his parents died when he was a boy. An uncle helped raise him on a farm.

Naismith studied at *McGill University* in Montreal. He played sports there, including rugby football. He also studied to become a minister. He hoped to help young people through both faith and sport.
In 1890 he moved to Springfield to train at the YMCA school. Soon he was teaching there too. He was about 30 years old when he made up basketball. He later became a medical doctor as well.

words.d: a university in Montreal, Canada, where Naismith studied
a leader and teacher in a Christian church

lessons.title: Two Peach Baskets
lessons.mainIdea: The first goals were two peach baskets nailed to a balcony rail ten feet above the gym floor.
reading: Naismith asked the school's building worker for two square boxes. The worker did not have any. He brought two old *peach baskets* instead. Naismith accepted them.

The gym had a running track that circled the room overhead. It worked like a *balcony*. Naismith nailed a basket to its lower rail at each end. The rail was ten feet high, so the goals were ten feet high.

The baskets still had bottoms. When a player scored, the ball stayed inside. Someone had to climb up and take it out. The first ball was not a special basketball. It was a soccer ball the gym already owned.

words.d: a woven basket made to carry peaches; the first basketball goal
a raised floor or walkway that hangs over part of a room

lessons.title: The First Game
lessons.mainIdea: Most accounts say the first basketball game was played in December 1891 by 18 students and ended 1 to 0.
reading: Naismith's class had 18 students. He split them into two *teams* of nine players each. That is almost twice as many players as a team uses today. Nine was simply half the class.
Springfield College and the Basketball Hall of Fame give the date as 21 December 1891. Players were not used to the new rules yet. Many *fouls* were called. A foul is a move the rules do not allow.
Most accounts say the game ended 1 to 0. A student named William R. Chase scored the only goal. The class liked the new game. Soon students in other gyms wanted to try it too.

words.d: a group of players who play together on one side
an action the rules do not allow, which brings a penalty

lessons.title: Thirteen Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith wrote thirteen rules for the new game and pinned them on a board in the gym.
reading: Before the first game, Naismith wrote out *thirteen rules*. He had them typed. Then he pinned the paper to a bulletin board near the gym door, where every player could read it.
The rules said the ball could be thrown in any direction. A player could not run while holding the ball. Shouldering, holding, pushing, tripping and striking another player were against the rules.

Naismith grew up with rough football. He wanted a game with less crashing into people. Rule 5 said a player who kept making fouls had to sit out until the next goal. The rules named a *referee* to judge the ball.

words.d: the first written rules of basketball, made by Naismith in 1891
the official who decides whether players follow the rules

lessons.title: Printed in The Triangle
lessons.mainIdea: On 15 January 1892, the school newspaper printed the thirteen rules, and they began to spread.
reading: The Training School had a student *newspaper* called The Triangle. On 15 January 1892, it printed Naismith's rules. The article was called "A New Game."
Printed rules can travel farther than a paper on a wall. Copies went out to YMCAs in other towns. Teachers there could read the rules and try the game in their own gyms.
Students who finished their training went to lead YMCAs in other cities. Many brought the new game with them. Within a few years, YMCA gyms across the United States had basketball.

words.d: printed pages of news that come out again and again
one piece of writing in a newspaper or magazine

lessons.title: Naming the Game
lessons.mainIdea: A student wanted to call the game Naismith Ball, but Naismith said no, and it became basket ball.
reading: At first the new game had no name. One student, Frank Mahan, said it should be called Naismith Ball. Naismith laughed and said no. He said a name like that would kill any game.
Mahan then pointed out that the game had a ball and a basket. So it could be called *basket ball*. Naismith agreed. For years people wrote it as two words.
Over time the two words joined into one: *basketball*. The peach baskets are long gone. But the name still remembers the first goals nailed to a balcony in Springfield.

words.d: the first way of writing the game's name, as two words

lessons.title: Where the Rules Are Now
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith's original typed rules sold for about $4.3 million in 2010 and are now kept at the University of Kansas.
reading: Naismith kept the typed pages of his thirteen rules. After he died in 1939, his family took care of them. The two typed pages are yellow and fragile now, more than a century later.
In 2010 the Naismith family sold the pages at an *auction*. David Booth, a graduate of the University of Kansas, paid about $4.3 million. He gave them a home at the school where Naismith had worked.
Springfield keeps the game's memory too. The Naismith Memorial Basketball *Hall of Fame* opened there in 1968. It honors players, coaches and others who shaped the game.

words.d: a sale where people offer money and the highest offer wins
a museum that honors the most important people in a field
